title: Optimisation globale structurée: propriétés, équivalences et résolution
contribution: PhD thesis that links structured global-optimization classes (MIP0-1, disjoint bilinear, BIL, concave QP, QQP, GLCP, linear maxmin, bilevel) through proven reformulations. It uses these links to prove that boundedness of disjoint bilinear programs is strongly NP-complete (PROHIBITION), to build a finite exact algorithm exploiting two symmetric maxmin reformulations, to introduce embedded algorithms (Beale-Small MIP B&B embedded in the Hansen et al. BLP algorithm), to enumerate all extreme Nash equilibria of bimatrix games up to 29x29 and 700x5, and to design a branch-and-cut for nonconvex QCQP with four minimax-error cut classes, applied to eight literature applications including Graham's octagon.
problem_entry: Field-level diagnosis: class-specific methods developed in parallel although classes share difficulty, so transfer tools (not only solutions) across classes via reformulations (pp. 19-20). Per-chapter gaps: BILD methods need compactness (p. 53); NP-equivalence hides practical difficulty differences (pp. 86-87); equilibrium enumeration limited to ~8x8 (pp. 114-116); QCQP generality and hardness (p. 129); heuristic answers of unknown precision (p. 173).
key_idea: A reformulation is a lens: study which properties survive it and move optimality conditions, bounds and tests across classes. Al(BILD) branches on complementarity of both symmetric maxmin reformulations for a balanced tree (pp. 45, 70-78); EEE specializes it to games (pp. 116-122); Al(QQP) refines outer approximations with cuts whose points minimize the maximum weighted error (pp. 136-156).
assumptions: Ch. 2: no compactness of feasible set or optimal value (p. 85); cuts assume X polytope and no PROHIBITION (p. 68). Ch. 1: big-L reformulations need L large enough, with numerical risk (p. 37). Ch. 4: no nondegeneracy needed, simplex vertices (pp. 113, 119). Ch. 5: minimization, no equalities in X, finite positive bounds on all variables, epsilon_r-epsilon_z-optimality target (pp. 130, 152-153).
proof_devices: reformulation defined by polynomial-time transfer of an optimal solution, not by polynomial transformation (Def. 1.2, p. 33)
integrality forced through a lower level: follower sets v = min{u, 1-u}, leader imposes v = 0 (Props 1.3, 1.11, pp. 35, 42)
counterexamples to tempting shortcuts: penalized GLCP->BLP fails for every finite L (Ex. 1.12, p. 43); large-L bounding box cannot replace the unboundedness test (p. 84)
strong NP-completeness of PROHIBITION by reduction from KERNEL (Thm 2.2, pp. 56-58)
normalization 1'u <= 1 turns a cone-unboundedness test into a bounded bilinear problem with a strict-positivity criterion (Prop. 2.4, pp. 58-59)
necessity by vertex-plus-ray decomposition of diverging sequences (Thm 2.8, pp. 61-62) with a 1-D example showing vertex-only tests are insufficient (Ex. 2.6, p. 60)
one-directional local-optimality transfer, counterexample to the converse, stronger hypothesis restoring it (Props 2.9, 2.11, Ex. 2.10, pp. 63-65)
gamma-extension through an inner minimization reduces to one optimization problem / an LP (Lemma 2.13, Cor. 2.14-2.15, pp. 67-69)
finiteness by counting variables fixed along each branch plus implicit enumeration of bases via complementarity (Thm 2.20, p. 78; Thm 4.1, pp. 120-122)
embedding proof by induction on the subproblem index, matching algorithms step by step and showing the richer algorithm's extra steps are redundant (Thm 3.6, pp. 96-97)
extreme point characterized by a singleton set of tight constraints (Thm 4.1, pp. 120-121)
minimax error equalization to choose linearization points, root selected by intermediate-value argument (Props 5.14-5.17, pp. 147-152)
finite convergence to epsilon-optimality because each child linearizes an interval of length epsilon_r/u_i acceptably (Thm 5.19, pp. 155-156)
experiments: C/CPLEX 2.1 and C++/CPLEX 4.0 on a SPARC SS20 (pp. 79, 125, 167-168). Ch. 2: generators with known optima counts, Floudas-Pardalos concave QPs (optimality of ST and Phillips-Rosen solutions confirmed), random sets of 10 instances with mean/std and real density, same-machine comparison vs a tuned Al(BLP) (about 14-80x more nodes where both rows are readable), sizes to 200+200 variables, ~30% time saved by root-only monotonicity relations, Thieu comparison declined (pp. 79-85). Ch. 4: Winkels' 6x2 example reveals an omitted equilibrium; random games to 29x29 and 700x5 with log-time plot (pp. 125-127). Ch. 5: 8 printed reformulated applications, two runs (cold vs optimum supplied), octagon certified to 4 decimals in 110 h by region exclusion (pp. 157-171).
positioning: Unifies bilevel, bilinear, MIP, game-theory and QCQP literatures (pp. 25-46, 50-54, 113-116, 131-133); sorts methods by what they need and guarantee (pp. 53-54); direct technical critiques: Vaish-Shetty's convergence claim called fallacious with the exact Weierstrass error (pp. 53-54), Ivanilov-Mukhamediev unstated hypothesis (p. 53), Mukhamediev redundancy (p. 115), Wen-Yang bound never better than LP relaxation (p. 105), Winkels' missed equilibrium (p. 125).
writing: French thesis; epigraph per chapter, Discussion section per chapter, roadmap and source-report pointers in each chapter intro (pp. 25, 49-50, 87, 113, 131); worked examples carry the hard concepts, including a two-column step-matched run with deliberately non-consecutive step letters (pp. 92, 98-100); calibrated hedging (il semble; suggests but does not suffice, p. 107).
limits_future: Limits: exponential growth (pp. 79, 82-83, 126-127), random-only game instances (p. 127), proof silent on running time (p. 156), approximate QCQP solutions without subclass structure (p. 172), octagon conditional on Graham's conjecture (pp. 170-171). Future: concavity cuts inside Al(BILD), embeddings for GLCP/cutting planes/Gomory cuts, Nash refinements, nonlinear cuts and fractional/polynomial specializations (pp. 108-109, 128, 174-175).

method_links.note: Proposer/certifier split inside exact B&B: Gauss-Seidel LP alternation gives incumbents while finiteness rests on complementarity branching; two-run protocol prices the incumbent; octagon uses a geometric warm start. Same split as card c01 (S015), which reuses the Ch. 5 solver.

Problem-class semantics before algorithm; the modeling decision whether the leader may empty the follower's feasible set switches LMM between bilevel and disjoint bilinear (unbounded) interpretations.

Counterexamples to tempting reformulations and shortcuts, failed converses with restoring hypotheses, necessary-and-sufficient conditions, audits of Vaish-Shetty, Ivanilov-Mukhamediev and Winkels. Variant in form: guarantees are finiteness/exactness/epsilon-optimality, not a stationarity ladder; proof admitted silent on time.
Engineering instances printed in full in the reformulated form solved, with epsilon-optimal solutions and a corrected typo from an earlier formulation; no online release or executable.

Currency is CPU time and nodes; fair-comparison moves present: same machine/language/libraries, competitor tuned, cross-machine and tolerance caveats, mean/std over 10 instances, meaningless comparison declined.
Per-chapter research codes; the Ch. 5 QCQP code later becomes the instrument of the pooling paper (card c01), but no long-lived solver yet.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: reformulation as a lens (transfer tests, not just solutions)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Stated aim to adapt tools across classes; Tomlin penalties ported to BLP; both symmetric maxmin reformulations used in one algorithm; conclusion on reformulations as viewpoint.
Def. 3.1 and Thm 3.6: Beale-Small MIP B&B generates the same subproblem sequence as the Hansen et al. BLP algorithm on the reformulation; converse left open; difficulty preorder proposed.
Each application run cold and with an epsilon-optimal solution supplied, motivated by fast heuristics without guarantees; second card with this pattern after S015 (c01).
Winkels' degenerate 6x2 example has an omitted extreme equilibrium; typo 9800 -> 98000 in Quesada-Grossmann's alkylation formulation.
Isolate whether a bounded optimum exists, prove it strongly NP-complete (PROHIBITION), answer it with the same engine on normalized auxiliary problems in Phase I.
Linearization points for four cut classes chosen by equalizing two error terms rather than bisecting; recalled in card c01 as an improvement of the 2000 algorithm.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: extremal-geometry side line: numeric global optimization first, exact algebraic certificate later
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Graham's unit-diameter octagon solved numerically to 4 decimals after 110 h, conditional on the conjectured configuration: the earliest instance of the small-polygon line (cf. card s03, S094).

transferable: Build a reformulation map between neighboring classes (reformulation = poly-time optimal-solution transfer) and, for each arrow, ask which optimality conditions and tests can be carried along (pp. 33-34, 174).
Prove two algorithms step-equivalent by induction on the subproblem index, show which steps of the richer one become redundant, then port the stronger test of one to the other (pp. 96-97, 103).
Turn an unboundedness-along-a-cone test into a bounded problem by adding 1'u <= 1 and testing strict positivity (pp. 58-59).

Before designing the main algorithm, check whether its precondition (bounded optimum) is itself hard: define the decision problem, reduce from a known NP-complete one, and reuse the main engine on auxiliary problems (pp. 56-58, 75-77).
Choose cut/linearization points by equalizing maximum weighted errors, e.g. a = (sqrt2-1)x + (2-sqrt2)sqrt(v) for the tangent to x^2, instead of bisecting (pp. 147-148).
Branch so each child fixes one object from each of two symmetric reformulations, and show the balance effect as a node-count ratio against a same-machine competitor (pp. 70, 82).
Give a competitor every advantage (same machine/language/libraries, tuned options) and say so (pp. 81-82); report small implementation trade-offs as numbers (p. 79).
For random instances report nominal and realized density, mean and std over 10 instances, and outliers (pp. 81, 125-126).
Run the exact method cold and with a known optimum supplied to separate search cost from proof cost (p. 168).
Certify a hard numeric optimum by a loose bracketing run, region exclusion one bound constraint at a time, then a tight run in the remaining box (pp. 170-171).
Print each application instance in the exact reformulated form solved, with tolerances and solution vector, and correct typos found in earlier formulations (pp. 157-167, 160).
Present two step-equivalent algorithms with aligned, deliberately non-consecutive step letters and one example in two parallel columns (pp. 92, 98-100).
After each correct result, add the smallest counterexample showing why the obvious simplification is invalid (pp. 43, 84).
coauthors: Sole-authored thesis (directors B. Jaumard and G. Savard, p. 3); chapter results joint with P. Hansen, B. Jaumard and G. Savard (refs [14]-[20], pp. 177-178)

quotes.text: Cette preuve de convergence théorique ne donne aucune indication sur le temps réel requis par l’algorithme.

Les modélisations actuelles sont souvent trop complexes pour une résolution précise par les méthodes existantes. Fréquemment, les méthodes proposées donnent des solutions approchées ou heuristiques, dont la précision est inconnue.
